entries.1:1: David had just returned to his town of Ziklag after defeating the Amalekites, and Saul was now dead. This sets the scene for the news David is about to receive.
entries.1:2: A man arrived from Saul's camp with torn clothes and dirt on his head, which were signs of mourning and defeat. He bowed down before David to show respect.
entries.1:3: David asked the man where he had come from, and the man replied that he had escaped from the Israelite army.
entries.1:4: David asked for a report on the battle, and the man told him the army had fled and many were dead, including Saul and his son Jonathan.
entries.1:5: David wanted to know how the man was so sure that Saul and Jonathan were dead.
entries.1:6: The man explained that he happened to be on Mount Gilboa and saw Saul leaning on his spear as enemy chariots and horsemen closed in on him.
entries.1:7: Saul looked back, saw the man, and called out to him, and the man answered that he was there.
entries.1:8: Saul asked who he was, and the man told him he was an Amalekite.
entries.1:9: Saul asked the man to come and kill him, saying he was in great pain but still alive.
entries.1:10: The man said he killed Saul because he was sure Saul wouldn't survive, and he brought Saul's crown and armband to David.
entries.1:11: David and all his men were overcome with deep grief and tore their clothes in mourning.
entries.1:12: They mourned and fasted until evening for Saul, Jonathan, and the fallen Israelites, because so many had died by the sword.
entries.1:13: David asked the young man where he was from, and he answered that he was the son of a foreigner, an Amalekite.
entries.1:14: David was angry that the man had no fear of killing the king whom God had specially chosen and anointed.
entries.1:15: David ordered one of his men to kill the Amalekite, and he did.
entries.1:16: David told the man that his own words condemned him, since he had admitted to killing God's anointed king.
entries.1:17: David composed a song of mourning for Saul and Jonathan.
entries.1:18: The song was written down in the Book of Jashar and was taught to the people of Judah.
entries.1:19: The song laments that Israel's heroes, the mighty leaders, have fallen and died on the hills.
entries.1:20: David didn't want the news spread to the Philistine cities, because Israel's enemies would celebrate and mock.
entries.1:21: David called for the mountains of Gilboa to have no dew or rain, since that is where Saul's shield and strength were dishonored.
entries.1:22: Saul and Jonathan fought bravely and effectively, never holding back their weapons from the enemy.
entries.1:23: Saul and Jonathan were loved and admired, inseparable in life and death, and they were swift and strong like eagles and lions.
entries.1:24: David called on the women of Israel to mourn Saul, who had brought them wealth and fine clothing.
entries.1:25: The song repeats its grief that mighty warriors have fallen, and that Jonathan has died on the hills.
entries.1:26: David expressed deep personal sorrow for Jonathan, whose friendship and love had been extraordinarily precious to him.
entries.1:27: The song closes by lamenting that the mighty have fallen and the weapons of war are broken.
entries.2:1: David asks God whether he should move into the towns of Judah, and God tells him to go, specifically to Hebron. It shows that David sought God's direction before making a big move, and God gave him a clear answer.
entries.2:2: David goes to Hebron and brings his two wives with him. This shows he was starting a new chapter of life there with his family.
entries.2:3: David brings all his men and their families to live in the towns around Hebron. His whole community moved together, not just him alone.
entries.2:4: The men of Judah anoint David with oil and make him king over their tribe, and David learns that the men of Jabesh-gilead had buried Saul. David is now publicly recognized as king, at least over part of the nation.
entries.2:5: David sends a message blessing the men of Jabesh-gilead for kindly burying Saul. He honors people who showed loyalty and kindness, even to a king who had been his enemy.
entries.2:6: David asks God to be good and faithful to them and promises to reward their kindness himself. He shows that good deeds done for others should be noticed and repaid.
entries.2:7: David tells them to be strong and brave, since Saul is dead and Judah has made him king. He encourages them not to be afraid and offers himself as their leader.
entries.2:8: Abner, the commander of Saul's army, takes Saul's son Ish-bosheth to a place called Mahanaim. He is setting up Saul's son as a rival leader.
entries.2:9: Abner makes Ish-bosheth king over the northern tribes of Israel. So now there are two competing kings: David in the south and Ish-bosheth in the north.
entries.2:10: Ish-bosheth was forty when he became king over Israel and ruled only two years, while Judah sided with David. His reign was short and limited, and David had the loyalty of the south.
entries.2:11: David ruled as king in Hebron over Judah for seven and a half years. This gives a clear timeline of how long David waited and ruled before things changed.
entries.2:12: Abner and the men of Ish-bosheth leave Mahanaim and go to Gibeon. This is the start of a military confrontation between the two sides.
entries.2:13: Joab and David's men meet Abner's group face to face at a pool in Gibeon, lining up on opposite sides. The two armies are now staring each other down.
entries.2:14: Abner suggests that some young men fight it out in front of them, and Joab agrees. A contest is arranged that will quickly turn deadly serious.
entries.2:15: Twelve men from each side step forward to fight. It's an even matchup that sets up a violent clash.
entries.2:16: Each man grabs his opponent by the head and stabs him, so all twenty-four die together, and the place is named the Field of Sides. What started as a contest ended in mutual slaughter.
entries.2:17: A fierce battle breaks out that day, and Abner and the men of Israel are beaten by David's men. The fighting escalates far beyond the original contest.
entries.2:18: Three of Zeruiah's sons are there—Joab, Abishai, and Asahel—and Asahel is very fast on his feet. Asahel's speed becomes important in what happens next.
entries.2:19: Asahel chases Abner directly, not swerving to the right or left. He is determined to catch Abner and won't be distracted.
entries.2:20: Abner looks back and asks if it's Asahel, and Asahel says yes. Abner now knows who is chasing him.
entries.2:21: Abner tells Asahel to go after someone else and take their weapons instead, but Asahel refuses to stop chasing him. Asahel's persistence puts him in serious danger.
entries.2:22: Abner warns Asahel again to turn aside, asking why he should have to kill him and be ashamed before Asahel's brother Joab. Abner doesn't want to kill him, but Asahel won't listen.
entries.2:23: Asahel keeps chasing, so Abner strikes him in the stomach with the back end of his spear, and Asahel dies; everyone who comes to that spot stops. Asahel's stubborn pursuit cost him his life.
entries.2:24: Joab and Abishai keep chasing Abner, and the sun sets as they reach a hill near the road through the wilderness of Geba. The pursuit continues into the evening.
entries.2:25: The men of Benjamin gather behind Abner and take their stand on top of a hill. Abner's side regroups to make a stand.
entries.2:26: Abner calls out to Joab, asking if the fighting will go on forever and pointing out it will only end bitterly, and urges him to stop the pursuit of fellow countrymen. He appeals for the killing to stop.
entries.2:27: Joab swears by the living God that if Abner hadn't spoken, the men would have kept chasing and fighting until morning. Joab agrees to stop because Abner spoke up.
entries.2:28: Joab has a horn blown, and all the people stop chasing Israel and fighting. The battle finally comes to an end.
entries.2:29: Abner and his men travel all night through the Arabah, cross the Jordan, and reach Mahanaim. They retreat safely back to their base.
entries.2:30: Joab returns from chasing Abner and counts his men, finding that nineteen of David's men besides Asahel are missing. The cost of the battle is counted.
entries.2:31: David's men had killed three hundred and sixty of Benjamin and Abner's men. David's side won a costly but decisive victory.
entries.2:32: They bury Asahel in his father's tomb in Bethlehem, and Joab and his men travel all night, reaching Hebron at dawn. The story closes with a burial and a long march home.
entries.3:1: A long struggle went on between the followers of Saul and the followers of David. Over time David's side kept growing stronger while Saul's side kept getting weaker, which shows how God's plan for David moved forward even through a drawn-out conflict.
entries.3:2: While David was living in Hebron, he had several sons by different wives, and this verse names the first one, Amnon. It simply records the start of David's family growing during that time.
entries.3:3: This lists David's second and third sons, Chileab and Absalom, along with their mothers. It shows that David took wives from different places, which was common for kings then but would later cause him trouble.
entries.3:4: Here are David's fourth and fifth sons, Adonijah and Shephatiah, each by a different mother. The list keeps track of his growing household in Hebron.
entries.3:5: The sixth son was Ithream, and the verse sums up that all these sons were born to David in Hebron. It marks the end of the list of children born to him there.
entries.3:6: While the war between the two sides continued, Abner, Saul's top general, was building up his own power among Saul's supporters. He was becoming the real force behind Saul's remaining family.
entries.3:7: Saul had a wife or concubine named Rizpah, and Ish-bosheth accused Abner of sleeping with her. Taking a king's woman was seen as a claim to the throne, so this was a serious charge.
entries.3:8: Abner exploded in anger at the accusation and reminded Ish-bosheth of all he had done to protect Saul's family instead of handing them over to David. He felt his loyalty was being repaid with an insult.
entries.3:9: Abner swears that God should punish him if he does not now do what the Lord swore to do. He is committing himself to carry out God's declared plan.
entries.3:10: Abner vows to take the kingdom away from Saul's family and give it to David over all Israel and Judah, from the far north to the far south. He is promising to switch sides and deliver the whole nation to David.
entries.3:11: Ish-bosheth was so afraid of Abner that he could not say a single word back. It shows that Abner, not the king, held the real power.
entries.3:12: Abner sent a message to David offering to make a deal and use his influence to bring all Israel over to David's side. He was now openly working to hand David the throne.
entries.3:13: David agreed to the deal but set one condition: Abner had to bring Saul's daughter Michal, David's first wife, when he came. Until then David refused to meet with him.
entries.3:14: David sent a message to Ish-bosheth demanding that Michal be returned to him, since he had paid a high bride-price for her. He was insisting on his rightful wife back.
entries.3:15: Ish-bosheth did as David demanded and took Michal away from her current husband, Paltiel. She was being handed back as part of the political arrangement.
entries.3:16: Paltiel followed Michal weeping all the way to Bahurim, until Abner told him to go home, and he did. It is a sad picture of a man losing his wife because of a deal between powerful men.
entries.3:17: Abner spoke to Israel's leaders, reminding them that they had wanted David as king before. He urged them to act on that desire now.
entries.3:18: Abner reminded them that the Lord had promised to use David to rescue Israel from the Philistines and from all their enemies. He framed the switch to David as obeying God's own word.
entries.3:19: Abner also persuaded the tribe of Benjamin, Saul's own tribe, and then went to Hebron to report to David what Israel and Benjamin had agreed to. He was lining up support on all sides.
entries.3:20: Abner arrived in Hebron with twenty men, and David held a feast for them. The welcome showed David accepted Abner's offer of peace.
entries.3:21: Abner promised to go and gather all Israel to make a covenant with David so his kingdom would be as large as he wished, and David sent him away in peace. The agreement seemed settled and friendly.
entries.3:22: Just then Joab and David's soldiers came back from a raid with a lot of plunder, and they found that Abner had already been sent away in peace. The timing set up a dangerous clash.
entries.3:23: Joab and his men were told that Abner had come to the king and had been sent away safely. Joab was not there when it happened, and he did not like what he heard.
entries.3:24: Joab went to David and questioned him sharply for letting Abner go. He was angry that such an important enemy had been allowed to leave freely.
entries.3:25: Joab accused Abner of coming only to spy on David, to learn his movements and everything he was doing. He was painting Abner's visit as a trick.
entries.3:26: After leaving David, Joab sent men to bring Abner back from the spring of Sirah, and they did so without David knowing. Joab was acting on his own behind the king's back.
entries.3:27: When Abner returned to Hebron, Joab took him aside by the town gate as if to speak privately and stabbed him in the stomach, killing him to avenge his brother Asahel. It was a cold-blooded murder disguised as a quiet conversation.
entries.3:28: When David heard what happened, he declared that he and his kingdom were innocent before the Lord of Abner's blood. He wanted it clear that he had no part in the killing.
entries.3:29: David called down a curse on Joab and his family, asking that trouble, disease, and violence never leave them. He was expressing how deeply he condemned the murder.
entries.3:30: The verse explains that Joab and his brother Abishai killed Abner because he had killed their brother Asahel in battle at Gibeon. It was revenge for a death in war.
entries.3:31: David ordered Joab and everyone with him to mourn publicly, wearing rough cloth, and the king himself walked behind the body. David was making a public show of grief and distancing himself from the killing.
entries.3:32: They buried Abner in Hebron, and the king and all the people wept loudly at his grave. The whole nation joined in mourning a leading man.
entries.3:33: The king composed a lament for Abner, asking whether he had died the way a fool dies. David was honoring Abner and pointing out that his death was not a fair fight.
entries.3:34: The song says Abner's hands were not tied and his feet were not chained, yet he fell as if struck down by wicked men, and the people wept again. It stressed that he was killed by treachery, not in open battle.
entries.3:35: The people urged David to eat while it was still daylight, but he swore an oath not to touch food until sunset. His refusal to eat showed how seriously he was grieving.
entries.3:36: Everyone noticed this and was pleased, just as they were pleased with everything the king did. David's conduct won the people's approval.
entries.3:37: That day it became clear to all Israel that the king was not behind Abner's death. David's public mourning convinced the nation of his innocence.
entries.3:38: The king told his servants to notice that a great leader and prince had fallen in Israel that day. He was acknowledging the seriousness of the loss.
entries.3:39: David admitted that even as king he felt weak, and that the sons of Zeruiah, Joab and Abishai, were too strong for him to control, so he left their punishment to the Lord. He was saying he could not deal with them himself and trusted God to repay their evil.
entries.4:1: When Ish-bosheth heard that his top general Abner had died, he lost his nerve and the whole nation panicked. It shows how quickly people fall apart when their support is gone, and reminds us that human security is fragile.
entries.4:2: Ish-bosheth had two raiding captains, Baanah and Rechab, who came from Beeroth in Benjamin's territory. These are the men the story will focus on next.
entries.4:3: The original people of Beeroth had fled to Gittaim and were still living there when this was written. This explains why these men had ties to that town.
entries.4:4: Jonathan's son Mephibosheth was only five when news came that Saul and Jonathan had died; his nurse grabbed him and ran, and he fell and became lame. It shows how one family's tragedy left a lasting mark on an innocent child.
entries.4:5: Rechab and Baanah went to Ish-bosheth's house at midday while he was resting, and the woman guarding the door had fallen asleep while cleaning grain. The scene is set for a sneak attack.
entries.4:6: The two brothers slipped inside without anyone noticing. Their plan was working because the house was unguarded.
entries.4:7: They found Ish-bosheth lying on his bed, killed him, cut off his head, and traveled all night through the valley. They murdered a sleeping man and carried off proof of it.
entries.4:8: They brought the head to David and claimed God had given him justice against Saul's family. They expected a reward, but they were really presenting the evidence of their own crime.
entries.4:9: David answered them by swearing on the living God, who had kept him safe through every danger. He was reminding them that he did not owe his safety to murder.
entries.4:10: David recalled that he had already executed a man who brought him news of Saul's death, thinking it would please him. That man got death, not a reward, for his news.
entries.4:11: David argued that if that was the reward for a messenger, then men who murder an innocent person in his own bed deserve far worse. He was determined to hold them accountable for the killing.
entries.4:12: David had the two men executed, their hands and feet cut off, and their bodies hung by the pool in Hebron, while Ish-bosheth's head was buried with Abner. David publicly rejected their crime and gave the dead man a proper burial.
entries.5:1: The tribes of Israel came to David and declared that they were his own relatives, sharing the same flesh and blood. This means the people finally accepted David as one of their own and were ready to follow him as king.
entries.5:2: They reminded David that even while Saul was king, David was the one who actually led Israel's armies in battle. They also recalled that God had chosen David to be the shepherd and ruler of his people, so his kingship was God's idea, not just a political deal.
entries.5:3: The elders of Israel met David at Hebron and made a formal agreement with him in God's presence, then anointed him king over the whole nation. This means David's rule was officially recognized and sealed with a covenant before God.
entries.5:4: David was thirty when he became king and ruled for forty years in total. This gives us a simple timeline of his reign and shows how long God sustained him as leader.
entries.5:5: He ruled over Judah from Hebron for seven and a half years, then over all Israel and Judah from Jerusalem for thirty-three years. This shows how his kingdom grew from one tribe to the whole nation.
entries.5:6: David and his men went to attack Jerusalem, which was held by the Jebusites, who taunted him that even their blind and lame could keep him out. The Jebusites were confident their city was too strong for David to capture.
entries.5:7: But David captured the stronghold of Zion, which became known as the City of David. Despite the taunts, God gave David the victory and a new capital.
entries.5:8: David told his men to attack through the water shaft and strike down the Jebusites, including the blind and lame who had mocked him. This became the reason for a saying that the blind and lame could not enter the house, likely referring to a custom about entering the temple area.
entries.5:9: David moved into the fortress and began building up the city around it, starting from the Millo. This means David made Jerusalem a real home and a growing capital for his kingdom.
entries.5:10: David kept growing stronger and more powerful because the Lord, the God of armies, was with him. His success came from God's presence, not just his own skill.
entries.5:11: Hiram, the king of Tyre, sent David cedar wood and skilled workers in wood and stone, and they built David a palace. This shows that even foreign kings recognized David's rising power and wanted to be on good terms with him.
entries.5:12: David understood that the Lord had established him as king and had made his kingdom great for the sake of God's people Israel. He saw his success as God's doing and as a blessing meant for the nation, not just for himself.
entries.5:13: After moving from Hebron, David took more wives and concubines in Jerusalem and had more sons and daughters. This records how his family grew, though having many wives was common for kings of that time.
entries.5:14: These are the names of the sons born to David in Jerusalem: Shammua, Shobab, Nathan, and Solomon. Listing them shows how David's family line was growing in the new capital.
entries.5:15: Ibhar, Elishua, Nepheg, and Japhia were also sons born to David in Jerusalem. The list continues to record David's growing family.
entries.5:16: Elishama, Eliada, and Eliphelet were the last of the sons named as born to David in Jerusalem. Together with the earlier names, this completes the record of his sons born there.
entries.5:17: When the Philistines heard that David had been made king over all Israel, they came looking for him, and David went down to his stronghold. The Philistines saw David's united kingdom as a threat and moved against him.
entries.5:18: The Philistines spread out across the valley of Rephaim. This shows they were positioning themselves for battle against David.
entries.5:19: David asked the Lord whether he should attack the Philistines and whether God would give him victory, and the Lord told him to go because he would certainly hand them over. David didn't rush into battle on his own; he sought God's direction first and got a clear yes.
entries.5:20: David defeated the Philistines at Baal-perazim and said the Lord had broken through his enemies like rushing water breaks through a wall, so the place was named after that. David gave God the credit for the victory and marked the spot with a name that remembered it.
entries.5:21: When the Philistines fled, they left their idols behind, and David and his men carried them away. This shows the Philistines' gods were powerless to help them, and David's men removed them as spoils of war.
entries.5:22: The Philistines came up again and spread out in the valley of Rephaim. They weren't finished yet and tried a second time to defeat David.
entries.5:23: David asked the Lord again, and this time God told him not to attack from the front but to go around behind them and come at them near the spice trees. God gave David a different plan for this battle, showing that we should keep asking him rather than assuming the last strategy always works.
entries.5:24: God told David that when he heard the sound of marching in the tops of the trees, he should move quickly, because the Lord had gone out ahead of him to defeat the Philistine army. God himself was leading the battle, and David's job was to follow his signal.
entries.5:25: David did exactly what the Lord commanded and defeated the Philistines all the way from Gibeon to Gezer. Because David obeyed God's specific instructions, God gave him a complete victory.
entries.6:1: David gathered thirty thousand of Israel's soldiers for a major event. This shows he was serious about bringing the ark of God back and used his full strength to do it.
entries.6:2: David and the people went to bring back the ark, the sacred chest that represented God's presence and bore his name. They were treating it as something holy and important, not just an object.
entries.6:3: They placed the ark on a new cart and set out from Abinadab's house, with his sons Uzzah and Ahio guiding the oxen. This seemed practical, but it was not the way God had said the ark should be carried.
entries.6:4: Uzzah walked beside the ark while his brother Ahio went in front of it. They were escorting the sacred chest on its journey.
entries.6:5: David and the Israelites celebrated with all their energy, using songs and many instruments. Their joy was loud and wholehearted as they worshiped God.
entries.6:6: When they reached a threshing floor, the oxen stumbled and Uzzah reached out to steady the ark. He acted on instinct to keep the holy object from falling.
entries.6:7: God struck Uzzah dead for touching the ark, because God had said it must not be handled. This is a sober warning that God is holy and not to be treated casually.
entries.6:8: David was upset and angry about what happened, and he named the place after the event. The memory of that day stayed with the people.
entries.6:9: David became afraid of the Lord that day and wondered whether it was safe to bring the ark near him. Awe and fear of God's power stopped him in his tracks.
entries.6:10: Instead of taking the ark into his own city, David had it taken to the house of Obed-edom. He chose to wait rather than risk another disaster.
entries.6:11: The ark stayed at Obed-edom's house for three months, and God blessed him and his whole household. God's presence brought good to the one who received it.
entries.6:12: When David heard that Obed-edom's household was being blessed because of the ark, he went to bring it into his city with celebration. Good news about God's blessing gave him courage to try again.
entries.6:13: After the men carrying the ark had taken just six steps, David offered a sacrifice. He was being careful and thankful, honoring God at each stage of the journey.
entries.6:14: David, wearing a simple linen garment, danced before the Lord with all his might. His worship was sincere and uninhibited, not concerned with looking dignified.
entries.6:15: David and the Israelites brought the ark up with shouts of joy and the sound of horns. The whole event was a loud, public celebration of God.
entries.6:16: Michal, Saul's daughter, watched from a window and saw David dancing and leaping, and she thought he looked foolish. She judged his worship by appearances rather than by his heart.
entries.6:17: They set the ark in the tent David had prepared for it, and David offered burnt offerings and peace offerings. This was a formal act of worship and dedication to God.
entries.6:18: After the offerings, David blessed the people in the name of the Lord Almighty. As their king, he spoke God's favor over the whole nation.
entries.6:19: David gave every man and woman in the crowd bread, wine, and a cake of raisins, then sent them home. He shared generously so everyone could celebrate the day.
entries.6:20: When David returned home to bless his family, Michal met him with sarcasm, mocking him for exposing himself before the servant girls. She attacked his worship as shameful rather than honoring it.
entries.6:21: David answered that he was dancing before the Lord, who had chosen him to rule over Israel instead of her father's family, and he would keep worshiping. He defended his worship as directed to God, not to impress people.
entries.6:22: David said he would humble himself even more and be looked down on, but the servant girls she mentioned would respect him. He cared more about God's honor than about his own dignity.
entries.6:23: Michal never had a child until the day she died. The text presents this as the outcome of her contempt toward David's worship.
entries.7:1: David finally had peace from his enemies and was settled in his own palace. It means rest and safety are gifts worth noticing, not just achievements.
entries.7:2: David noticed he lived in a fine cedar house while God's sacred chest sat in a tent. It means he wanted to honor God better than he was doing.
entries.7:3: Nathan told the king to go ahead with his plan because God seemed to be with him. It means good leaders can still be wrong when they speak too quickly without asking God.
entries.7:4: That same night God spoke to Nathan. It means God steps in to correct our plans, even good ones, when they are not what he wants.
entries.7:5: God asked David whether he was really the one to build him a house. It means God does not need us to build him anything; he sets the terms, not us.
entries.7:6: God reminded David that since leaving Egypt he had never had a house but had traveled in a tent. It means God is not confined to buildings and has always been close to his people wherever they are.
entries.7:7: God asked whether he had ever demanded a cedar house from any leader of Israel. It means God had never asked for a grand building, so David's plan was his own idea, not God's command.
entries.7:8: God reminded David that he had taken him from tending sheep to lead Israel. It means God is the one who lifts ordinary people into places of responsibility.
entries.7:9: God said he had been with David everywhere and had defeated his enemies, and would make his name great. It means success comes from God's presence, not just from our own effort.
entries.7:10: God promised to plant Israel in their own land where they would be safe and no longer troubled. It means God cares about lasting security for his people, not just temporary relief.
entries.7:11: God promised David peace from his enemies and told him that God himself would establish a royal line for him. It means the greatest gift here is God's promise, not David's building project.
entries.7:12: God said that after David died, one of his own descendants would take the throne and his kingdom would be made strong. It means God's plans reach beyond one person's lifetime.
entries.7:13: This descendant would build a house for God's name, and God would make his throne secure forever. It means God himself would build an enduring kingdom through David's line.
entries.7:14: God would be a father to this king, and if he did wrong God would discipline him like a father corrects a son. It means God's family relationship includes loving correction, not rejection.
entries.7:15: God promised not to withdraw his mercy from this descendant as he had from Saul. It means God's commitment is steady even when people fail.
entries.7:16: God promised David's family and kingdom would last forever and his throne would never be overturned. It means God's promise to David was permanent, pointing to a king whose reign never ends.
entries.7:17: Nathan reported all these words and the vision to David. It means a faithful messenger simply passes on what God said, without adding or softening it.
entries.7:18: David sat before the Lord and asked who he was that God had brought him this far. It means real humility comes from realizing how much God has done for us.
entries.7:19: David said this was a small thing to God, who had also spoken about his family's distant future. It means God's generosity goes far beyond what we ask or expect.
entries.7:20: David said he had nothing more to say because God already knew him completely. It means we can be honest before God, who knows us better than we know ourselves.
entries.7:21: David said God had done this great work because of his own word and heart. It means God's promises rest on his character, not on our worthiness.
entries.7:22: David declared that God is great and there is no one like him. It means worship flows from recognizing who God truly is.
entries.7:23: David marveled that no other nation had a god who rescued them, made them his own, and drove out enemies for them. It means God's rescue of Israel was unique and showed his power and love.
entries.7:24: God made Israel his own people forever and became their God. It means belonging to God is a lasting relationship he establishes, not something we earn.
entries.7:25: David asked God to keep the promise he had made about him and his family. It means we can pray boldly for what God has already promised.
entries.7:26: David wanted God's name to be honored forever and David's family to be established. It means our deepest desire should be God's reputation, not just our own success.
entries.7:27: David said that because God had revealed his promise, he dared to pray this way. It means God's word gives us confidence to come to him in prayer.
entries.7:28: David affirmed that God is God, his words are true, and he had promised this good thing. It means we can trust God's promises because his character backs them up.
entries.7:29: David asked God to bless his family line forever, since God himself had said it. It means we can rest in God's blessing because it depends on his word, not our performance.
entries.8:1: David defeated the Philistines and captured their main city, which had been a stronghold against Israel. This shows God giving David success over a long-time enemy of his people.
entries.8:2: David defeated the Moabites and decided which of them would live and which would die, and the survivors became his servants. It was a harsh wartime victory that made Moab subject to him.
entries.8:3: David defeated Hadadezer, the king of Zobah, as that king was trying to extend his power toward the Euphrates River. This was one of David's victories that expanded Israel's control.
entries.8:4: David captured many of Hadadezer's chariot horses and soldiers, and he crippled most of the horses so they could not be used for war. He kept only enough for a small number of chariots.
entries.8:5: When Syrian forces from Damascus came to help Hadadezer, David defeated them too, killing many of their soldiers. This shows how far David's military reach extended.
entries.8:6: David stationed soldiers in Damascus and made the Syrians subject to him, and the writer notes that the Lord gave David victory wherever he went. The credit for David's success is given to God, not just to David.
entries.8:7: David took the gold shields carried by Hadadezer's officers and brought them back to Jerusalem. These became part of the wealth he later dedicated to God.
entries.8:8: David also took large amounts of bronze from two towns belonging to Hadadezer. This bronze would later be useful for building and temple work.
entries.8:9: Tou, the king of Hamath, heard that David had defeated the whole army of Hadadezer. This news led him to approach David.
entries.8:10: Tou sent his son to David to greet him and congratulate him, since Hadadezer had been Tou's enemy too, and he brought gifts of silver, gold, and bronze. These gifts showed Tou wanted peace with the powerful David.
entries.8:11: David set apart these gifts, along with silver and gold taken from other nations, as holy to the Lord. He treated the spoils of war as something to honor God with.
entries.8:12: This lists the nations David defeated and the goods he took from them, including Edom, Moab, Ammon, the Philistines, Amalek, and Hadadezer. It summarizes the source of the wealth he dedicated to God.
entries.8:13: David gained a great reputation after defeating eighteen thousand Edomites in the Valley of Salt. His victories made him famous among the surrounding nations.
entries.8:14: David placed soldiers throughout Edom and made the Edomites subject to him, and again the writer says the Lord gave David victory everywhere. The repeated phrase emphasizes that God was behind David's success.
entries.8:15: David ruled over all Israel and made fair decisions for all his people. This describes him as a king who cared about justice, not just conquest.
entries.8:16: This names Joab as commander of the army and Jehoshaphat as the official who kept records. It shows David organized a government with responsible officials.
entries.8:17: Zadok and Abiathar served as priests, and Seraiah served as secretary. These roles kept worship and administration running in David's kingdom.
entries.8:18: Benaiah commanded David's special guard troops, and David's sons served in priestly roles. This shows the key people David trusted to lead his household and army.
entries.9:1: David wants to show kindness to anyone left in Saul's family, and he does it because of his promise to his friend Jonathan. It shows that keeping promises and showing mercy to people who can't repay you matters.
entries.9:2: Saul's former servant Ziba is brought to David, and the king confirms who he is. This sets up the story: God can use even a servant to connect people who need help with someone who can give it.
entries.9:3: David asks if anyone from Saul's family is left so he can show them God's kindness, and he learns Jonathan has a son who can't walk. It reminds us that people with disabilities are often overlooked, but God sees them and so should we.
entries.9:4: Ziba tells David the man is staying in Lo-debar with Machir. The place was far from the palace, showing that this forgotten heir was living in obscurity until someone looked for him.
entries.9:5: David sends for Jonathan's son and has him brought from Lo-debar. It shows that kindness often takes action, not just good intentions, and that a powerful person can reach out to someone helpless.
entries.9:6: Mephibosheth comes to David, bows low to honor the king, and answers when David calls his name. It shows proper respect, and also that David treats him as a person, not just a name on a list.
entries.9:7: David tells him not to be afraid, promises to be kind because of Jonathan, gives back Saul's land, and invites him to eat at the king's table always. It's a picture of grace: undeserved kindness that restores what was lost and gives lasting honor.
entries.9:8: Mephibosheth bows again and calls himself a dead dog, meaning he feels worthless and unworthy of such attention. It's honest humility, and it shows that receiving kindness can feel overwhelming when you think you deserve nothing.
entries.9:9: David calls Ziba and gives all of Saul's property to Mephibosheth. It shows the king making the gift official and real, not just a nice feeling, and it puts the former servant in charge of managing it.
entries.9:10: Ziba, his sons, and his servants are told to farm the land so Mephibosheth has food, while Mephibosheth himself always eats at the king's table. It shows that practical work supports the gift, and that the one who receives grace still gets to sit at the king's table.
entries.9:11: Ziba agrees to do everything the king ordered, and Mephibosheth eats at David's table like one of the king's own sons. It shows that kindness can raise someone from a low place to a place of honor and belonging.
entries.9:12: Mephibosheth has a young son named Mica, and everyone in Ziba's household serves Mephibosheth. It shows the family line continues and that the kindness given to one person also blesses the next generation.
entries.9:13: Mephibosheth lives in Jerusalem and eats at the king's table regularly, even though he can't use his feet. It shows that his disability didn't keep him from the king's table, and that lasting kindness gives someone a real place to belong.
entries.10:1: The king of Ammon died, and his son Hanun took over as king. This is just setting the scene for what happens next.
entries.10:2: David wanted to show kindness to Hanun because Hanun's father had been kind to David, so he sent messengers to comfort him about his father's death. It shows David's goodwill toward a neighboring nation.
entries.10:3: The Ammonite leaders convinced Hanun that David's messengers were really spies scouting the city to destroy it. Their suspicion turned a friendly gesture into a reason for conflict.
entries.10:4: Hanun humiliated David's messengers by shaving off half their beards and cutting their clothes short, then sent them away. This was a public insult meant to shame them and David.
entries.10:5: David heard what happened and told the shamed men to stay in Jericho until their beards grew back, then return. He was protecting them from further embarrassment.
entries.10:6: The Ammonites realized they had made David an enemy, so they hired thousands of soldiers from several Aramean groups to fight for them. They prepared for war out of fear of the consequences.
entries.10:7: When David heard about the hired army, he sent his general Joab with all his best fighting men. David responded to the threat with full force.
entries.10:8: The Ammonites lined up at the city gate, while the hired Aramean soldiers positioned themselves out in the open field. The enemy forces were split into two groups.
entries.10:9: Joab saw he was surrounded, with enemies in front and behind, so he picked his best troops to face the Arameans. He made a quick, smart plan for a difficult situation.
entries.10:10: Joab put the rest of the army under his brother Abishai to face the Ammonites. He divided his forces to deal with both threats at once.
entries.10:11: Joab agreed with his brother that if one group was losing, the other would come help. They planned to support each other in the battle.
entries.10:12: Joab encouraged his men to be brave and fight for their people and their God's cities, while leaving the outcome to God. It's a call to do your best and trust God with the results.
entries.10:13: Joab and his men attacked the Arameans, who ran away in defeat. Their courage paid off in a quick victory.
entries.10:14: When the Ammonites saw their allies running, they also fled back into their city, so Joab stopped fighting and returned to Jerusalem. The battle ended with Israel winning.
entries.10:15: The Arameans regrouped after losing to Israel. Defeat didn't stop them from trying again.
entries.10:16: Hadadezer called in more Aramean troops from across the river, led by his army commander Shobach, and they gathered at Helam. The enemy was building up a larger force.
entries.10:17: David heard about this and gathered all Israel, crossed the Jordan, and met the Arameans at Helam, where they attacked him. David took the initiative to face the threat directly.
entries.10:18: The Arameans fled from Israel, and David's army killed seven hundred chariot crews and forty thousand foot soldiers, and wounded Shobach so that he died. It was a major victory for Israel.
entries.10:19: When the kings under Hadadezer saw they had lost, they made peace with Israel and served them, and the Arameans were too afraid to help Ammon anymore. Israel's victory ended the threat and secured peace.
entries.11:1: Spring was the normal season for kings to lead their armies out to war, and Israel's army was off fighting while David stayed behind in Jerusalem. Staying home when he should have been leading set up the trouble that follows.
entries.11:2: One evening David got up from resting and walked on his palace roof, where he saw a beautiful woman bathing. A casual look became the start of a serious wrong.
entries.11:3: David asked who she was and learned she was Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah the Hittite, one of his own soldiers. Knowing she was married should have stopped him right there.
entries.11:4: David sent for her and slept with her, then she went home. He used his power as king to take another man's wife.
entries.11:5: She became pregnant and sent word to David, so he could not keep the affair hidden. The consequences of his choice were now out in the open.
entries.11:6: David sent word to Joab, the army commander, to send Uriah back to him. He was already working on a plan to cover up what he had done.
entries.11:7: When Uriah arrived, David asked how the war and the soldiers were doing, making polite conversation. He was pretending to care while hiding his real motive.
entries.11:8: David told Uriah to go home and rest, and even sent a gift after him, hoping he would sleep with his wife. That way the pregnancy could be blamed on Uriah instead of David.
entries.11:9: Uriah did not go home; he slept at the entrance of the king's house with the other servants. His sense of duty spoiled David's cover-up plan.
entries.11:10: When David heard Uriah had not gone home, he asked him why, since he had just come from a long journey. David was frustrated that his plan was not working.
entries.11:11: Uriah said he could not enjoy home and his wife while his fellow soldiers and the ark were camped in the open field, and he swore he would not do it. He showed loyalty and self-control that the king lacked.
entries.11:12: David told Uriah to stay one more day and then he would send him back. David was stalling, still trying to find a way to hide his sin.
entries.11:13: David invited Uriah to eat and drink with him and got him drunk, hoping he would then go home to his wife. But even drunk, Uriah again slept with the servants and did not go home.
entries.11:14: The next morning David wrote a letter and sent it with Uriah to Joab. Uriah carried his own death sentence without knowing it.
entries.11:15: The letter ordered Joab to put Uriah at the front of the fiercest fighting and then pull back so he would be killed. David arranged the murder of a loyal soldier to cover his own sin.
entries.11:16: Joab followed the order and placed Uriah where he knew the enemy's strongest fighters were. He cooperated in David's plan.
entries.11:17: The men of the city came out and fought, and some of David's soldiers died, including Uriah the Hittite. David's plan worked, but at the cost of innocent lives.
entries.11:18: Joab sent David a report of everything that had happened in the battle. He had to explain the deaths, including Uriah's.
entries.11:19: Joab told the messenger to give the king the full report of the battle first. He was preparing how to break the news.
entries.11:20: Joab warned that the king might get angry and ask why the soldiers went so close to the city, where archers on the wall could shoot them. He expected David to question the tactics.
entries.11:21: Joab told the messenger that if the king asked, he should remind him how Abimelech was killed by a woman dropping a stone from a wall, and then say that Uriah was among the dead. Mentioning Uriah would end the king's anger.
entries.11:22: The messenger went and reported to David, and David got angry and asked the same questions Joab had predicted about going too near the wall. David was acting, since he already knew the plan.
entries.11:23: The messenger explained that the enemy came out against them, but they pushed them back to the city gate. He was building up to the bad news.
entries.11:24: He said the archers shot from the wall and some of the king's servants died, including Uriah the Hittite. The news David was waiting for finally arrived.
entries.11:25: David told the messenger to reassure Joab, saying deaths in war are normal, and to press the attack harder and take the city. David brushed off the loss of life, including the man he had murdered.
entries.11:26: When Bathsheba heard her husband was dead, she mourned for him. She grieved the loss of her husband.
entries.11:27: After the mourning ended, David brought her into his house and married her, and she had a son. But God was not pleased with what David had done.
entries.12:1: God sent the prophet Nathan to confront King David with a story about two men in one town, one rich and one poor. It sets up a trap to make David judge himself before Nathan names his sin.
entries.12:2: The rich man owned huge numbers of sheep and cattle. His abundance shows how little he needed to take from anyone else.
entries.12:3: The poor man had just one little lamb that he raised like a child, sharing his food, drink, and bed. This shows how deeply the poor man loved the one thing he had.
entries.12:4: When a guest came to the rich man, he refused to use any of his own animals and instead took the poor man's beloved lamb to feed the visitor. This is the injustice that makes the story so shocking.
entries.12:5: David burned with anger and swore that the man deserved to die. He judged the case rightly without realizing he was condemning himself.
entries.12:6: David added that the man must repay four times over because he showed no mercy. His verdict was fair, and it set up Nathan's coming accusation.
entries.12:7: Nathan told David plainly that he was the rich man in the story. Then he reminded David that God had made him king and protected him, so his sin was against a generous God.
entries.12:8: God had given David great wealth, power, and family, and would have given even more. David had no excuse for taking what belonged to someone else.
entries.12:9: Nathan asked why David had ignored God's word and done evil by having Uriah killed and taking his wife. The sin was not just against a man but against God himself.
entries.12:10: Because David showed contempt for God and took another man's wife, violence would never leave his family. Sin brings consequences that reach beyond the moment.
entries.12:11: God announced that trouble would rise from within David's own household, and his wives would be taken publicly. The judgment would match the secret wrong he had done.
entries.12:12: David acted in secret, but God said the consequences would happen openly before all Israel. Hidden sin does not stay hidden from God.
entries.12:13: David admitted his sin, and Nathan told him God had forgiven him so he would not die. Confession brings real mercy, though it does not erase every result.
entries.12:14: Even though David was forgiven, his contempt for God would still cost the child's life. Forgiveness and consequences can both be real at the same time.
entries.12:15: Nathan went home, and God struck the child David had with Uriah's wife so that he became very sick. The story turns from confrontation to grief.
entries.12:16: David pleaded with God for the child, fasting and lying on the ground all night. He poured out his desperate hope that God might spare the boy.
entries.12:17: His senior servants tried to get him up and to eat with them, but he refused. His grief was so deep that he would not be comforted.
entries.12:18: On the seventh day the child died, and the servants were afraid to tell David because they feared what he might do to himself. They had watched how intensely he had grieved.
entries.12:19: David noticed the servants whispering and guessed the child was dead, and they confirmed it. He read the truth from their behavior.
entries.12:20: David got up, washed, changed clothes, worshiped at the house of the Lord, and then ate. His grief turned into trust and acceptance of God's will.
entries.12:21: The servants asked why he fasted and wept while the child lived but ate once the child died. They did not understand the change in his behavior.
entries.12:22: David explained that while the child was alive he fasted and wept because he hoped God might show mercy and let the child live. He had prayed as long as there was hope.
entries.12:23: Now that the child was dead, fasting could not bring him back; David said he would go to the child one day, but the child would not return. He accepted death as final and looked ahead to reunion.
entries.12:24: David comforted Bathsheba, and she bore a son named Solomon, whom the Lord loved. God brought new life and hope after the grief.
entries.12:25: God sent word through Nathan to give the child the name Jedidiah, meaning loved by the Lord. This confirmed God's special favor on Solomon.
entries.12:26: Joab was fighting against Rabbah, the Ammonite city, and captured its water supply. The war moved forward while David's personal story unfolded.
entries.12:27: Joab sent messengers to tell David he had taken the water-town. He reported progress and asked for the king's next move.
entries.12:28: Joab urged David to gather the rest of the troops and finish taking the city himself, so the victory would be credited to the king rather than to Joab. He was protecting David's honor.
entries.12:29: David gathered all the people, went to Rabbah, fought against it, and captured it. He completed the victory Joab had started.
entries.12:30: David took the crown of Milcom from the king's head, a heavy gold crown set with precious stones, and it was placed on David's head, and he carried off much plunder. The victory brought wealth and symbolized the defeat of the Ammonite god.
entries.12:31: David put the people of the city to forced labor with saws, iron picks, axes, and brickmaking, and did the same to other Ammonite towns, then returned to Jerusalem. This shows the harsh reality of ancient warfare and the total subjection of the defeated.
entries.13:1: Amnon, one of King David's sons, became obsessed with his half-sister Tamar, who was very beautiful. This sets up a story of desire that turns destructive, warning us how unchecked longing can lead to terrible harm.
entries.13:2: Amnon's obsession made him physically sick, and because Tamar was off-limits to him, he felt trapped and frustrated. It shows how wanting what we cannot rightly have can eat away at us.
entries.13:3: Amnon had a friend named Jonadab, described as clever or shrewd. His cleverness turns out to be the kind that helps someone do wrong, reminding us that bad advice from friends can lead us into disaster.
entries.13:4: Jonadab noticed Amnon looked worse each day and asked what was wrong, and Amnon admitted he wanted Tamar. Being honest about a wrong desire is only the first step; what we do with it next matters most.
entries.13:5: Jonadab told Amnon to fake illness and ask his father to send Tamar to prepare food for him. This was a sneaky plan to get her alone, showing how a trusted friend can help set up a terrible wrong.
entries.13:6: Amnon followed the plan, pretending to be sick and asking the king to send Tamar to make him food. He used his father's trust to get what he wanted, which is a warning about how deception often hides behind normal-seeming requests.
entries.13:7: David, unaware of the plot, sent Tamar to Amnon's house to care for her sick brother. An innocent person was sent straight into danger because the king trusted his son's story.
entries.13:8: Tamar went to Amnon's house and made cakes for him right in front of him as he lay in bed. She was doing a kind, family duty, with no idea what he was planning.
entries.13:9: When she brought the food, Amnon refused it and told everyone else to leave the room. He was clearing the way to be alone with her, a sign that his intentions were not about food at all.
entries.13:10: Amnon asked Tamar to bring the food into his bedroom so he could eat from her hand, and she went in. She trusted him as her brother, which makes what follows a betrayal of that trust.
entries.13:11: When she came close to give him the food, Amnon grabbed her and told her to come to bed with him. This is the moment his hidden plan became an open assault.
entries.13:12: Tamar pleaded with him, saying this was shameful and evil and must not be done in Israel. She named the wrong clearly and tried to stop it, showing courage even when she was in danger.
entries.13:13: Tamar pointed out that both of them would be disgraced, and suggested he ask the king instead. She was trying to reason her way out of danger, but the person hurting her was not willing to listen.
entries.13:14: Amnon ignored her words, overpowered her, and forced himself on her. The text is blunt about what happened: this was rape, a serious crime and a deep betrayal of his sister.
entries.13:15: Right after the assault, Amnon hated Tamar even more intensely than he had wanted her before, and he told her to get out. This shows that lust is not love; it can turn into hatred once the desire is satisfied.
entries.13:16: Tamar said that sending her away now was an even greater wrong than what he had already done, and he still refused to listen. She was left with no protection and no justice from the one who had hurt her.
entries.13:17: Amnon called his servant and ordered him to throw her out and lock the door behind her. He treated her like something to be discarded, adding humiliation to the harm he had already done.
entries.13:18: Tamar was wearing the special long robe that the king's unmarried daughters wore, and the servant pushed her out and locked the door. The robe marked her as a royal virgin, so being cast out in it made her shame public.
entries.13:19: Tamar put ashes on her head and her hand on her head and went away crying loudly, which were traditional signs of deep grief and shame. She did not hide what had happened; she mourned openly because she had been deeply wronged.
entries.13:20: Absalom asked if Amnon had been with her, told her to stop crying and not to take it to heart, and she lived on in his house, still desolate. His words tried to quiet the matter rather than bring justice, and Tamar was left without comfort.
entries.13:21: When David heard what had happened he was very angry, but he did nothing to punish Amnon because he loved him as his firstborn. A father's anger without action left the wrong unaddressed and set the stage for more trouble.
entries.13:22: Absalom said nothing to Amnon, good or bad, but he hated him for what he had done to Tamar. Silence can hide deep anger that is waiting for a chance to strike.
entries.13:23: Two years later, Absalom held a sheep-shearing feast near Ephraim and invited all the king's sons. The long delay shows his hatred had not faded; he was waiting for the right moment.
entries.13:24: Absalom invited the king and his servants to the feast. On the surface it looked like a normal, generous invitation, but Absalom had a hidden purpose.
entries.13:25: The king declined, saying too many people would be a burden, and blessed him. David had no idea what Absalom was really planning.
entries.13:26: Absalom then asked that Amnon go instead, and the king wondered why Amnon in particular should go. This question shows David sensed something odd but did not stop it.
entries.13:27: Absalom kept pressing until the king let Amnon and all his sons go with him, and Absalom prepared a great feast. The trap was now set with the king's own permission.
entries.13:28: Absalom told his servants to strike Amnon down when he was drunk and cheerful, and to be brave about it. He used a celebration as cover for murder, turning a feast into a killing.
entries.13:29: Absalom's servants killed Amnon as ordered, and all the other king's sons jumped on their animals and fled. One act of revenge sent the whole royal family into panic.
entries.13:30: While they were still traveling, a false report reached David that Absalom had killed all his sons and none were left. Rumors in a crisis can multiply fear far beyond the truth.
entries.13:31: The king rose in grief, lay on the ground, and all his servants stood by with their clothes torn. This was the customary way to show overwhelming sorrow, and David believed the worst had happened.
entries.13:32: Jonadab, the same shrewd friend from before, told David not to believe all the sons were dead, since only Amnon was killed and Absalom had planned it since the day Amnon violated Tamar. He correctly explained the cause, showing that the earlier wrong had been left to fester.
entries.13:33: Jonadab urged the king not to think all his sons were dead, because only Amnon had died. His words were meant to calm the king, though the news was still terrible.
entries.13:34: Absalom fled, and a watchman saw a large group coming down the hillside and reported it to the king. The approaching crowd turned out to be the surviving sons, not an army.
entries.13:35: Jonadab told the king that the king's sons were arriving just as he had said. His prediction was confirmed, which showed he understood the situation better than the panicked king.
entries.13:36: As he finished speaking, the king's sons arrived weeping loudly, and the king and all his servants wept bitterly too. The whole family was overwhelmed with grief over Amnon's death and the chaos in their house.
entries.13:37: Absalom fled to Talmai, king of Geshur, and stayed there three years. He escaped punishment but lived in exile, separated from his family and his home.
entries.13:38: David mourned for his son the whole time Absalom was away. Even though Absalom had done wrong, David's grief shows how deeply family love can ache.
entries.13:39: David's heart longed for Absalom, and he was eventually comforted over Amnon's death. The story shows a father torn between grief, anger, and love, with no easy way to make things right.
entries.14:1: Joab could tell that King David was starting to miss his son Absalom and wanted him back. It shows that even when someone has been wronged, love can soften over time.
entries.14:2: Joab found a clever woman from Tekoa and told her to dress and act like someone in deep mourning for the dead. He was setting up a story to get the king to change his mind.
entries.14:3: Joab gave the woman the exact words to say to the king. He was using her to make his case without speaking to David directly.
entries.14:4: The woman came to the king, bowed low to show respect, and begged him for help. She was playing the part of a desperate widow.
entries.14:5: The king asked what was wrong, and she told him she was a widow whose husband had died. She was drawing him into her story step by step.
entries.14:6: She claimed her two sons fought in a field with no one to stop them, and one killed the other. This was a made-up story designed to mirror David's own situation with Absalom.
entries.14:7: She said her whole family wanted the surviving son put to death for killing his brother, which would leave her with no one to carry on the family name. The story was meant to make David see his own family situation.
entries.14:8: The king told her to go home and promised he would give orders to protect her. He was responding to her story without realizing it was really about him.
entries.14:9: She said if there was any guilt in sparing the son, let it fall on her and her family, not on the king. She was making it easier for him to show mercy.
entries.14:10: The king promised that if anyone bothered her about it, he would make sure they left her alone. He was committing himself to protect her case.
entries.14:11: She pressed him to swear before God that no one would harm her son, and the king swore that not a hair on his head would be hurt. She had gotten him to promise mercy in a case of killing.
entries.14:12: She asked for permission to say one more thing, and the king told her to go ahead. She was about to turn the story toward his own situation.
entries.14:13: She pointed out that the king was being unfair to God's people by not bringing back the son he had sent away, since he had just promised mercy in her made-up case. She was gently showing him his inconsistency.
entries.14:14: She reminded him that everyone dies eventually and can't be brought back, and that God doesn't want a banished person cut off forever. She was urging David to bring Absalom home while there was still time.
entries.14:15: She said she came to speak because she was afraid of the people, and she hoped the king would grant her request. She was wrapping up her appeal.
entries.14:16: She said the king would listen and rescue her and her son from those who wanted to destroy them and cut them off from God's people. She was flattering him as a protector.
entries.14:17: She praised the king, saying his judgment was like that of an angel of God, able to tell good from bad. She was building him up so he would act on her words.
entries.14:18: The king asked her to answer honestly and hold nothing back, and she agreed to speak. He was starting to suspect something.
entries.14:19: The king asked if Joab was behind all this, and she admitted that Joab had told her what to say. She couldn't deny it once he asked directly.
entries.14:20: She said Joab did this to change the situation, and she praised the king's wisdom as being like an angel's, knowing everything on earth. She was still flattering him even while admitting the plot.
entries.14:21: The king told Joab he would do it and told him to go bring the young man Absalom back. David finally gave in and allowed his son to return.
entries.14:22: Joab bowed down and blessed the king, saying he was glad to know he had the king's favor because his request was granted. He was relieved his plan had worked.
entries.14:23: Joab went to Geshur and brought Absalom back to Jerusalem. Absalom was finally allowed to come home.
entries.14:24: The king said Absalom could go to his own house but must not come to see him. So Absalom was back in the city but still cut off from his father.
entries.14:25: Absalom was the best-looking man in all Israel, praised for his appearance from head to foot. His good looks made him stand out among the people.
entries.14:26: He cut his hair once a year because it got so heavy, and it weighed about two hundred shekels by the king's standard. This detail shows how remarkable his hair was.
entries.14:27: Absalom had three sons and a daughter named Tamar, who was very beautiful. He had a family of his own.
entries.14:28: Absalom lived in Jerusalem for two full years without ever seeing his father's face. He was home but still shut out from the king.
entries.14:29: Absalom sent for Joab to ask him to take a message to the king, but Joab wouldn't come, even when he sent a second time. Joab was ignoring him.
entries.14:30: So Absalom told his servants to set Joab's barley field on fire, and they did. He was forcing Joab to pay attention to him.
entries.14:31: Joab came to Absalom's house and asked why his servants had burned his field. Absalom had gotten the reaction he wanted.
entries.14:32: Absalom said he had called for Joab so he could send him to the king to ask why he had been brought back if he still couldn't see his father, and he offered to be put to death if he had done wrong. He wanted a real answer from David.
entries.14:33: Joab told the king, and when David sent for Absalom, Absalom came and bowed low before him, and the king kissed him. Father and son were finally reconciled, at least on the surface.
entries.15:1: Absalom started acting like a king by getting a chariot, horses, and fifty men to run ahead of him. He was building his own importance and popularity, which is a warning about pride and self-promotion.
entries.15:2: Absalom got up early and stood by the city gate, where people came for legal cases, and asked each visitor where they were from. He was deliberately meeting people and gaining their attention for his own purposes.
entries.15:3: Absalom told each person their case was good and right, but claimed the king had no one to hear them. He was flattering people and making the king look neglectful so they would side with him.
entries.15:4: Absalom wished out loud that he were the judge, promising he would give everyone justice. He was offering people what they wanted in order to win their loyalty.
entries.15:5: When people came to bow to him, Absalom took them by the hand and kissed them. He acted warm and familiar to make people feel important and draw them to himself.
entries.15:6: Absalom did this to everyone who came to the king for judgment, and in this way he stole the loyalty of the people of Israel. He was quietly turning the nation against David.
entries.15:7: After four years Absalom asked the king for permission to go to Hebron to fulfill a vow. He used a religious excuse to cover what he was really planning.
entries.15:8: Absalom explained that while he lived in Geshur he had promised to worship the Lord in Hebron if he was allowed back in Jerusalem. His words sounded devout, but they were part of his scheme.
entries.15:9: The king told him to go in peace, and Absalom left for Hebron. David trusted him and did not see the danger behind the request.
entries.15:10: Absalom secretly sent messengers through all the tribes to announce, at a signal, that he was now king in Hebron. He was organizing a rebellion while pretending to be loyal.
entries.15:11: Two hundred men from Jerusalem went with Absalom without knowing anything about his plan. They were innocent people caught up in his scheme.
entries.15:12: Absalom sent for Ahithophel, one of David's advisers, while he was offering sacrifices, and his conspiracy grew as more people joined him. A trusted adviser turning against David made the rebellion much stronger.
entries.15:13: A messenger came to David and told him that the hearts of the men of Israel had turned to Absalom. David learned that his own son had won over the nation.
entries.15:14: David told his servants they must flee at once or none of them would be safe from Absalom, who might attack the city quickly. He chose to leave rather than risk a massacre in Jerusalem.
entries.15:15: The king's servants told him they were ready to do whatever he decided. They showed their loyalty to David in a moment of crisis.
entries.15:16: The king left with all his household, except ten of his concubines, who were left to take care of the house. David had to abandon his home and most of his possessions.
entries.15:17: The king and all his servants went out and stopped at a place called the Far House. This was the beginning of David's flight from Jerusalem.
entries.15:18: All the people passed by him, including the Cherethites, the Pelethites, and six hundred men from Gath who had come with him. These were loyal soldiers who stayed with David.
entries.15:19: The king asked Ittai from Gath why he was coming along, since he was a foreigner far from his own land. David was giving him a chance to go back to safety.
entries.15:20: David told Ittai he had only just arrived and should not have to wander with him, and he wished him mercy and faithfulness from the Lord. David showed kindness and did not want to drag a newcomer into his trouble.
entries.15:21: Ittai swore by the living Lord and by the king's life that wherever David went, whether to life or death, he would stay with him. He showed remarkable loyalty and courage.
entries.15:22: David told Ittai to go forward, and Ittai went on with all his men and the little ones with them. David accepted his loyalty and let him join the journey.
entries.15:23: Everyone wept loudly as the people passed by, and the king stood in the Kidron Valley while the people went toward the wilderness. The whole scene was one of grief and loss.
entries.15:24: Zadok and Abiathar came with the ark of God and set it down until all the people had passed by. The priests brought the most sacred object to be with David in his flight.
entries.15:25: David told Zadok to take the ark back into the city, saying that if the Lord was pleased with him, he would return to see it again. David trusted God's will rather than using the ark as a good-luck charm.
entries.15:26: David said that if the Lord had no delight in him, he was still ready to accept whatever God chose to do. He submitted himself to God's decision, whether good or bad for him.
entries.15:27: The king told Zadok the priest to go back to the city in peace with his son Ahimaaz and Abiathar's son Jonathan. David arranged for loyal men to stay behind in Jerusalem.
entries.15:28: David said he would wait at the crossing in the wilderness until he received news from them. He set up a way to get information while he was away.
entries.15:29: So Zadok and Abiathar took the ark back to Jerusalem and stayed there. They obeyed David and remained in the city as he had asked.
entries.15:30: David went up the Mount of Olives weeping, with his head covered and his feet bare, and all the people with him wept too. These were signs of deep sorrow and humiliation as he fled.
entries.15:31: David was told that Ahithophel was among Absalom's supporters, and he prayed that the Lord would turn Ahithophel's advice into foolishness. David turned to God for help against a clever enemy.
entries.15:32: When David reached the top of the slope where people worshiped God, Hushai the Archite came to him in grief with dust on his head. Hushai came as a loyal friend in a time of distress.
entries.15:33: David told Hushai that if he went with him he would only be a burden. David was thinking practically about what would help him most.
entries.15:34: David told Hushai to go back and pretend to serve Absalom, saying he would be Absalom's servant just as he had been his father's, so he could work against Ahithophel's plans. David set up a secret plan to protect himself.
entries.15:35: David reminded Hushai that Zadok and Abiathar the priests were in the city, and told him to report anything he heard from the king's house to them. David built a network of trusted people to pass information.
entries.15:36: David pointed out that the two priests had their sons with them, Ahimaaz and Jonathan, and said Hushai could send messages to David through them. This gave David a reliable way to receive news.
entries.15:37: So Hushai, David's friend, went into the city just as Absalom arrived in Jerusalem. Hushai went back to do the dangerous work David had asked of him.
entries.16:1: Ziba, who served Mephibosheth, met David as he fled with donkeys loaded with food and wine. It shows someone bringing supplies to a king in a desperate moment.
entries.16:2: David asked why he had brought all this, and Ziba said the donkeys were for riding and the food and drink were for his tired men. The gifts were meant to help the king's group survive their journey.
entries.16:3: David asked where Mephibosheth was, and Ziba claimed he had stayed in Jerusalem hoping to get his father's kingdom back. Ziba was accusing his master of betrayal.
entries.16:4: David believed Ziba and gave him everything that belonged to Mephibosheth, and Ziba bowed in thanks. It shows how quickly a king under pressure could make a costly decision based on one report.
entries.16:5: As David reached Bahurim, a man from Saul's family named Shimei came out and cursed him. Someone from the family of the king David had replaced was publicly wishing him harm.
entries.16:6: Shimei threw stones at David, his officials, and his soldiers on both sides. He was attacking the king openly while the king's men stood around him.
entries.16:7: Shimei cursed David and called him a man of blood and a worthless man. He was accusing David of being violent and evil.
entries.16:8: Shimei said God was punishing David for the blood of Saul's family and had given the kingdom to Absalom, so David was caught in his own evil. He was claiming David's troubles were deserved.
entries.16:9: Abishai offered to go over and cut off Shimei's head for cursing the king. He wanted to defend David's honor by force.
entries.16:10: David refused, telling the sons of Zeruiah to leave Shimei alone, since he believed the Lord had told Shimei to curse him. David chose to accept the insult rather than fight back.
entries.16:11: David told his men that if his own son wanted him dead, a man from Saul's family cursing him was no surprise, so they should let him continue. He saw the cursing as something God had allowed.
entries.16:12: David hoped the Lord would see his suffering and repay him with good for the curses he received that day. He was trusting God to notice his pain and respond.
entries.16:13: David and his men kept traveling while Shimei walked along the hillside nearby, cursing and throwing stones and dust at him. The harassment continued as they moved on.
entries.16:14: The king and his people arrived at the Jordan River exhausted and rested there. After the stress and travel, they finally got a chance to stop and recover.
entries.16:15: Absalom and the men of Israel came into Jerusalem, and Ahithophel was with him. The rebellion had now taken over the capital city.
entries.16:16: Hushai, David's friend, came to Absalom and greeted him with shouts of long life to the king. He appeared to switch sides, though he was really still loyal to David.
entries.16:17: Absalom asked Hushai why he had not gone with his friend David. He was testing whether Hushai was really on his side.
entries.16:18: Hushai said he would be loyal to the man whom the Lord and the people had chosen as king, and he would stay with him. He was giving Absalom a reason to trust him.
entries.16:19: Hushai added that just as he had served Absalom's father, he would now serve Absalom. He was making his loyalty to the new king sound natural.
entries.16:20: Absalom asked Ahithophel for advice on what they should do next. The new king was looking for a plan to secure his position.
entries.16:21: Ahithophel told Absalom to sleep with his father's wives who were left in charge of the house, so all Israel would hear that he was hated by his father and his supporters would be encouraged. The advice was meant to make the break between father and son permanent.
entries.16:22: They set up a tent on the roof for Absalom, and he went in to his father's women in front of all Israel. This publicly shamed David and showed everyone that Absalom had taken over.
entries.16:23: In those days Ahithophel's advice was treated as if it came from God himself, and both David and Absalom valued it that way. People regarded his counsel as extremely reliable.
entries.17:1: Ahithophel offers to take a large force and chase David down that same night. It shows how quickly David's enemies wanted to strike while he was weak.
entries.17:2: Ahithophel plans to attack David while he is exhausted and catch him off guard, so his followers will scatter and only the king will be killed. The plan aims to end the conflict by targeting one man.
entries.17:3: Ahithophel promises that once David is dead, everyone will come back to Absalom peacefully. He frames the whole war as being about one man's life.
entries.17:4: Absalom and his advisors liked this plan. It seemed like a smart and quick way to win.
entries.17:5: Absalom decides to get a second opinion before acting. He calls for Hushai to hear what he thinks.
entries.17:6: Absalom tells Hushai the plan and asks whether they should follow it or hear another idea. He is weighing his options.
entries.17:7: Hushai says Ahithophel's plan is not wise this time. He is about to argue against it.
entries.17:8: Hushai warns that David and his men are experienced fighters and are furious, like a mother bear robbed of her cubs. He also notes David won't be sleeping among the troops, so he'll be hard to surprise.
entries.17:9: Hushai says David is probably hiding in a cave or some secret spot. If Absalom's men get beaten at first, rumors will spread that his side is losing.
entries.17:10: Even brave soldiers would lose their nerve, because everyone knows David and his men are fierce fighters. Fear would spread through the army.
entries.17:11: Hushai advises gathering the whole nation into one huge army and having Absalom lead it himself. He wants a massive show of force rather than a quick raid.
entries.17:12: With that many men, they could find David wherever he hides and overwhelm him completely. Hushai promises total victory.
entries.17:13: Even if David hides in a walled town, Hushai says the whole army could drag the town into the valley until nothing is left. He paints a picture of overwhelming force.
entries.17:14: Absalom and his men prefer Hushai's plan over Ahithophel's. But the real reason is that God was working to defeat Absalom by making the smarter plan fail.
entries.17:15: Hushai tells the priests Zadok and Abiathar both plans—what Ahithophel advised and what he himself advised. He is passing on information to David's allies.
entries.17:16: Hushai urges them to send word to David right away: don't camp across the river, cross it immediately or you'll be destroyed. He wants David to escape while there's time.
